```{r}

library(tidyverse)
library(repurrrsive)
library(jsonlite)
```


# Importing `.csv` files

## Importing a `.csv` {.smaller}

This should be straightforward, right?

```{r}
co2 <- read_csv("data/monthly_in_situ_co2_mlo.csv")
co2
```

::: {.callout-caution title="What do you notice?"}
Look closely at the output. Do the column names and the first rows look the way you expect?
:::


## The power of `read_csv()` {.smaller}

Have a look at `?read_csv`. These arguments solve most import problems:

| Argument | What it controls |
|------|----------------------|
| `quote` | The character that wraps text fields (default: a double quote) |
| `escape_backslash` | Whether a backslash escapes special characters (default: `FALSE`) |
| `col_names` | Use the first row as names (`TRUE`), generate names (`FALSE`), or supply your own |
| `col_types` | Tell R each column's type instead of letting it guess |
| `col_select` | Read only some of the columns |
| `id` | Add a column holding the file path (useful with several files) |
| `na` | Which values count as missing (default: blank and `"NA"`) |
| `name_repair` | How to fix problem column names (duplicates, blanks, spaces) |

## Putting the arguments to work

```{r eval=FALSE}
read_csv(
  "myfile.csv",
  col_names = c("id", "group", "score"),  # supply names if the file has none
  col_types = cols(id = col_character()), # control how a column is read
  na = c("", "NA", "-99"),                # also treat -99 as missing
  col_select = c(id, score)               # keep only these columns
)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Why this matters"}
The default behaviour guesses. When the guess is wrong, these arguments let you tell R what the file really contains.
:::


# Several files at once

## Read multiple files into a single data frame

If several `.csv` files have the **same columns** (and the same column names), `read_csv()` can read them all into one data frame.

::: {.callout-tip title="Keep the filenames with `id =`"}
Store the filename in a column. If anything goes wrong with the data, it is easier to trace the problem back to its source.
:::

## Reading three files at once {.smaller}

```{r}
sales_files <- c(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hadley/r4ds/refs/heads/main/data/01-sales.csv",
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hadley/r4ds/refs/heads/main/data/02-sales.csv",
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/hadley/r4ds/refs/heads/main/data/03-sales.csv"
)
read_csv(
  sales_files,      # the list of filenames to read from
  id = "file"       # a new column named "file" keeps track of the filename
)
```

## When a file does not exist

```{r}
read_csv("https://pos.it/r4ds-04-sales")
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Cryptic error messages"}
If a file does not exist, the error message can be hard to read. It depends on what the other end sends back.
:::

## Read every file in a folder

Typing every filename gets old. `list.files()` collects them for you:

```{r eval=FALSE}
list.files("./", pattern = "\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE)
```

Combine it with `read_csv()` to import the whole folder:

```{r eval=FALSE}
csv_files <- list.files("./", pattern = "\\.csv$", full.names = TRUE)
read_csv(csv_files, id = "file")
```

::: {.callout-note title="A regular expression"}
The `pattern` is a **regular expression**. Here, `\\.csv$` means "ends in `.csv`".
:::


# Writing data

## Write a data frame to file

Corresponding to the `read_` functions, there are `write_` functions. Start with `?write_` in the Console.

- We discuss two here:
  - `write_csv()` (the partner of `read_csv()`)
  - `write_parquet()` (the partner of `read_parquet()`)

::: {.callout-note title="It does not matter where the data frame comes from"}
`write_` functions convert any data frame into the right format to save. For example, `read_excel()` can read an Excel file into a data frame, and `write_csv()` can write that data frame back out as a `.csv`.
:::

## Using `write_csv()`

This saves the `test` data frame as a `.csv` in the same folder as this `.qmd` file.

```{r eval=FALSE}
output_file <- "test.csv"
write_csv(test, output_file)
```

::: {.callout-caution title="A drawback"}
The **type information** for each column is lost. When you read the file back with `read_csv()`, you need to set all the types up again.
:::

## Shout out for `parquet` files {.smaller}

`write_parquet()` (from the `arrow` package) saves *everything* in the data frame, including column types.

```{r eval=FALSE}
library(arrow)
write_parquet(test, "test.parquet")
read_parquet("test.parquet")      # recovers the data frame exactly
```

| | `.csv` | `.parquet` |
|---|--------|------------|
| Keeps column types | No | Yes |
| Open in a text editor | Yes | No (it is *binary*) |

::: {.callout-note title="No pain, no gain"}
You get exact recovery, but you give up the ability to read the file in a simple text editor.
:::


# Importing spreadsheets

## Excel files {.smaller}

The packages `readxl` and `writexl` deal with Excel files.

| Function | What it does |
|----------|--------------|
| `read_xls()` | Reads Excel files in `xls` format |
| `read_xlsx()` | Reads Excel files in `xlsx` format |
| `read_excel()` | Reads both `xls` and `xlsx` |
| `write_xlsx()` | Writes a data frame in `xlsx` format |

::: {.callout-note title="Writing may change the file"}
`write_xlsx()` may produce a file slightly different from the one you read in, even if you read it from a `.xlsx` file.
:::

## Getting started and other packages

- Reading local Excel files is quite similar to reading `.csv` files
- Run `?read_excel` in the Console, or see the [textbook](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/spreadsheets#sec-reading-spreadsheets-excel)
- The `openxlsx` package (textbook [2e, Section 21.2.8](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/spreadsheets#formatted-output)) can also read `xlsx` files, especially remote ones

::: {.callout-caution title="Different conventions"}
`openxlsx` follows slightly different conventions from the tidyverse style used in `readxl`. Look things up with `?` in the Console if unsure.
:::


# Importing deeply nested data: JSON

## What is JSON?

::: {.callout-note title="Definition"}
**JSON** stands for **J**ava**S**cript **O**bject **N**otation. It is a very common format for getting data from a web server.
:::

- A JSON **object** is a set of *key-value pairs*, separated by commas, inside `{}`
- A JSON **array** is a comma-separated list inside `[]`, such as `[1, 3, 4]`
- Objects and arrays can be **nested** inside each other

## What a JSON object looks like

One repository from our example file (shortened):

```json
{
    "id": 61160198,
    "name": "after",
    "full_name": "gaborcsardi/after",
    "owner": {
        "login": "gaborcsardi",
        "id": 660288,
        "type": "User",
        "site_admin": false
    },
    "private": false,
    "description": "Run Code in the Background",
    "language": "R",
    "stargazers_count": 5,
    "default_branch": "master"
}
```

Notice that `owner` is **another object inside** the object.

## Packages and an example file {.smaller}

```{r eval=FALSE}
library(repurrrsive)
library(jsonlite)
```

`repurrrsive` comes with a `gh_repos.json` file on your hard drive. This function gives its location:

```{r}
gh_repos_json()
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Open it in a text editor"}
Navigate to the file and open it. It is a (nested) **array**, and each entry in the innermost array is a complicated JSON **object**.
:::

## Reading the file into R

Use `read_json()` (from `jsonlite`) with the location of the file:

```{r}
gh_repos <- gh_repos_json() |> read_json()
```

The file has to do with GitHub repository information. In the same folder there are other `.json` files and matching `.xml` files.

## Do not print it!

::: {.callout-warning title="It is HUGE"}
Typing `gh_repos` displays the whole thing, which is very long and very confusing.
:::

```{r eval=FALSE}
gh_repos
```

Use `View()` instead. It shows the structure **and** the data:

```{r eval=FALSE}
View(gh_repos)
```

::: {.callout-note title="RStudio only"}
`View()` is specific to RStudio.
:::

## What did `View()` show?

- `gh_repos` is a **list of lists**
- Each entry has many key-value pairs
- The `owner` field contains **another object** inside

A more universal tool is `str()`, which describes the **str**ucture of an object. The option `max.level` lets you look inside it in stages.

## Drilling down: top level {.smaller .scrollable}

```{r}
gh_repos |> 
  str(max.level = 1)
```

## Drilling down: one level down {.smaller .scrollable}

```{r}
gh_repos[[4]] |>
  str(max.level = 1)
```

## Drilling down: one more level {.smaller .scrollable}

```{r}
gh_repos[[4]][[1]] |>
  str(max.level = 1)
```

## Drilling down: into the `owner` field {.smaller .scrollable}

```{r}
gh_repos[[4]][[1]][["owner"]] |> 
  str(max.level = 1)
```


# Rectangling with `unnest_` functions

## The plan

We have a complicated JSON array in R. We want a **data frame**.

- Start with `tibble()` to get a data frame
- Use `unnest_longer()` and `unnest_wider()`, depending on the structure to be unwrapped

::: {.callout-note title="Rectangling"}
Turning nested data into a rectangular data frame (rows and columns) is called **rectangling**.
:::

## Step 1: `tibble()` {.smaller}

```{r}
gh_repos_df_raw <- tibble(gh_repos)
gh_repos_df_raw
```

This gives a tibble based on the first level of the array. Each row is another **array** of objects.

## Step 2: `unnest_longer()` {.smaller}

Each entry in the array becomes a **row**:

```{r}
gh_repos_df_level1 <- gh_repos_df_raw |>
  unnest_longer(gh_repos)         # try unnest_wider for effects
gh_repos_df_level1
```

Each row now holds a JSON **object**, not an array.

## Step 3: `unnest_wider()` {.smaller}

Each field in the object becomes a **column**:

```{r}
gh_repos_df_level2 <- gh_repos_df_level1 |>
  unnest_wider(gh_repos)            # try unnest_longer for effects
gh_repos_df_level2
```

## Step 4: unwrap `owner` {.smaller}

This is almost a data frame, but `owner` still holds lists. Another `unnest_wider()` resolves it.

```{r}
gh_repos_df_level3 <- gh_repos_df_level2 |> 
  unnest_wider(
    owner,
    names_sep = "_"            # comment out this to see the effect
  )
gh_repos_df_level3
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Use `names_sep`"}
It attaches `owner` to the names of the subfields, so the new column names are explicit.
:::

## Checkpoint: longer or wider?

::: {.callout-important title="Think about it"}
- `unnest_longer()` turns each entry of an **array** into a **row**
- `unnest_wider()` turns each field of an **object** into a **column**

Look at `[1, 3, 4]` and at `{"id": 1, "name": "after"}`. Which function would you use for each?
:::

## Putting it together {.smaller}

From the file location to a data frame, in one pipeline:

```{r}
gh_repos_location <- gh_repos_json()

gh_repos_df <- gh_repos_location |>
  read_json() |>
  tibble() |>
  rename(items = `read_json(gh_repos_location)`) |>  # stop prior to this to see why
  unnest_longer(items) |>
  unnest_wider(items) |>
  unnest_wider(owner, names_sep = "_")

gh_repos_df
```

It is easier to see the data with `View()`:

```{r eval=FALSE}
View(gh_repos_df)
```

## Now we can plot

Once the data is tidy, we can plot it:

```{r}
gh_repos_df |>
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = log10(watchers), y = log10(size))) +
  geom_jitter(mapping = aes(color = owner_login))
```



# When the JSON is a single object

## A different situation

`gh_repos` is a **list** of JSON objects, so `tibble()` turned it into a tibble with one row per entry.

If the file is exactly **one** JSON object, `tibble()` behaves differently. We can simulate this by taking a single object out of `gh_repos`:

```{r}
gh_repos_1 <- gh_repos[[1]][[1]]
```

```{r eval=FALSE}
View(gh_repos_1)
```

## The problem {.smaller .scrollable}

```{r}
tibble(data = gh_repos_1)
```

::: {.callout-warning title="The field names are missing"}
We get a tibble with one column, whose rows are the fields of the object. The most unsatisfying part is that the **names of the fields are completely missing**.
:::

## The fix {.smaller .scrollable}

Force the single object into a `list` with one entry **before** making the tibble:

```{r}
(single_object <- tibble(data = list(gh_repos_1)))
```

Then `unnest_wider()` gives a one-row tibble, with each field as a column:

```{r}
single_object |>
  unnest_wider(col = data)
```


# Wrap-up

## Choosing the right tool {.smaller}

| Format | Read | Write | Good to know |
|--------|------|-------|--------------|
| `.csv` | `read_csv()` | `write_csv()` | Plain text, but column types are lost |
| Parquet | `read_parquet()` | `write_parquet()` | Binary, keeps column types |
| Excel | `read_excel()` | `write_xlsx()` | Packages `readxl` and `writexl` |
| JSON | `read_json()` | | Nested; needs rectangling with `unnest_` functions |

## Key takeaways

::: {.incremental}
- `read_csv()` has many arguments; use them when the default guess is wrong
- Use `id =` to keep track of which file each row came from
- `write_csv()` loses column types; `parquet` keeps them
- JSON is nested: look at the structure with `View()` or `str()` first
- Rectangle with `tibble()`, then `unnest_longer()` (rows) and `unnest_wider()` (columns)
:::
